list.listitem: The Federal Advisory Committee on Heritable Disorders in Newborns and Children lists sickle cell disease (SCD) in their Recommended Uniform Screening Panel, a list of 38 disorders for which they recommend universal newborn screening. Most states screen newborns for these disorders. C

Screen all patients for conditions as recommended by the United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) along with specific sickle cell conditions including stroke, retinopathy, pulmonary hypertension, kidney disease, liver disease, and osteoporosis. B

Screen children ages 2 to 16 years for cerebrovascular disease using transcranial Doppler and provide long-term transfusion therapy to prevent stroke in children with abnormal transcranial Doppler velocity and oral prophylactic penicillin for children up to age 5 years to prevent pneumonia.A
Provide pneumococcal, meningococcal, hepatitis B and influenza vaccination. B

Drug therapy for pain includes NSAIDs, rapid initiation of opioids during a crisis, and adjuvant pain medications.B Consider use of 1000 mg omega-3 fish oil to reduce the frequency of vaso-occlusive crises. B

Complications of sickle cell anemia include acute stroke, venous thromboembolism, priapism, pulmonary hypertension, acute chest syndrome (ACS), leg ulcers, splenic sequestration, acute renal failure, avascular necrosis and proliferative sickle retinopathy. C

In adults with 3 or more severe vasoocclusive crises during a year, with pain or chronic anemia that interferes with usual activities, or with severe or recurrent ACS hydroxyurea therapy is strongly recommended. It is also recommended for infants, children and adolescents without regard to the presence of symptoms (moderate strength).B

Regular blood transfusions can reduce the risk of subsequent cerebrovascular accidents in patients with a history of stroke or children with silent cerebral infarcts and should be considered for children with elevated transcranial Doppler velocity. B
Consider HLA-matched related hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in patients with SCD who experienced a stroke, recurrent episodes of ACS, frequent pain. C

background.definition: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is an inherited hemoglobinopathy in which a sickling hemoglobin (HbS or HbC) has been substituted for normal hemoglobin (HbA). In sickle cell anemia, both copies of the beta-hemoglobin gene are HbS. SCD includes other sickle hemoglobinopathies such as sickle thalassemia and hemoglobin SCD.

list.listitem: The 2021 estimated incidence rate in the United States was 33.6 per 100.000 live births, which correspond to 1,220 babies born that year with SCD.
Based on Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates, 1 out of every 365 African American or Black person is born with SCD and about 1 every 13 is born with sickle cell trait.

According to the CDC, the exact number of people living with SCD in the United States is unknown. The CDC estimates about 100,000 Americans living with SCD, 90% of which are non-Hispanic Black or African American, and 3-9% Hispanic or Latino.
A more recent estimate from the Global Burden of Disease Study concluded that in 2021 approximately 60,000 Americans were affected by SCD.
The disease primarily affects people who have ancestry from sub-Saharan Africa. It also occurs in people with Mediterranean, South Asian, and Arabian ancestry.

Based on data from the US Nationwide Inpatient Sample, there were 216 (95% confidence interval (CI) 173.3-258.7) SCD-related hospitalizations per 100,000 US blacks in 1998 and 178.4 (95% CI 144.2-212.5) in 2008, but no consistent yearly decrease.

In 2016, there were 134,000 SCD-related inpatient hospital stays of which over three-fourths involved a pain crisis (HCUP Statistical Brief #251). Aggregate costs for these stays totaled $811.4 million, with an average length of stay of 5 days. Importantly, one-third of stays for SCD had a 30-day readmission (vs. 12.5% for non-SCD-related stays).
Each hospitalization cost approximately $6223 in 2004, accounting for $488 million.
SCD is the most common inherited hemoglobinopathy.
Morbidity and mortality are significant for this life-long disease. Many patients also have significant psychosocial and economic challenges.

One small case control study found sensorineural hearing loss in 37% of patients with SCD (mean age, 26 years) but no hearing loss among case-matched controls. In a meta-analysis of 21 studies, pooled prevalence of sensorineural hearing loss was 20.5% (95% CI 10.3-33).

Sickle cell trait is associated with an increased risk of hematuria, renal papillary necrosis, splenic infarction, exertional rhabdomyolysis, exercise-related sudden death, and it is exclusively associated with rare but often fatal renal medullary cancer.
There appears to be a higher incidence rate of COVID-19 among patients with SCD at 17.22 per 100,000 person-day, respectively, to June 15 2020.
Individuals with SCD have lower hemoglobin A1C levels than those without SCD despite similar mean fasting glucose and 2-hour glucose values, making this test less accurate.

SCD appears to be protective against human immunodeficiency virus (OR 0.25) and slows disease progression (OR 0.23). Implicated mechanisms include autosplenectomy, reduced CCR5 expression, and increased expression of heme and iron-regulated genes
SCD is an autosomal recessive inherited hemoglobinopathy.
Sickle hemoglobin results from a mutation that substitutes the amino acid valine for glutamic acid in the beta-hemoglobin chain.
Hemoglobin S forms polymers when deoxygenated.
The polymers form rigid fibers that align and distort the red blood cell.
Sickled red blood cells lead to micro- and macro-vaso-occlusion.
Vaso-occlusion causes intermittent ischemic episodes that lead to tissue damage and necrosis.

Endothelial activation by sickle-RBCs and other inflammatory mediators results in the activation of the endothelial lining of blood vessels which produces a pro-inflammatory environment. Specific pathways in this process are discussed in detail in a recent review.
Pain associated with SCD is thought to be a complex process that involves interactions with the vascular endothelium, as well as contributions from hemolysis, inflammation, and coagulation.
Chronic hemolytic anemia and recurrent vaso-occlusive episodes lead to acute and chronic end-organ damage.
Host susceptibility for vascular complications in one meta-analysis was associated with mutant genotypes (CT+TT vs. CC) of the MTHFR 677C>T polymorphism.

Most states provide universal screening for sickle cell diease (SCD). The Federal Advisory Committee on Heritable Disorders in Newborns and Children lists sickle cell disease (SCD) in their Recommended Uniform Screening Panel, a list of 38 disorders for which they recommend universal newborn screening. Most states screen newborns for these disorders. C

Screen all patients for conditions as recommended by the USPSTF along with specific sickle cell conditions, including stroke, retinopathy, pulmonary hypertension, kidney disease, liver disease, and osteoporosis. B
Provide pneumococcal, meningococcal, hepatitis B and influenza vaccination. B
Perform annual transcranial Doppler examinations for children with SCD, aged 2 to 16 years. B
NHLBI guidelines recommend penicillin prophylaxis for children under age 5 years to prevent pneumococcal infection. B

In adults with three or more severe vasoocclusive crises during a year, with pain or chronic anemia that interferes with usual activities, or with severe or recurrent acute chest syndrome (ACS) hydroxyurea therapy is strongly recommended. It is also recommended for infants, children and adolescents without regard to the presence of symptoms (moderate strength).B
The Health Resources and Services Administration Discretionary Advisory Committee on Heritable Disorders in Newborns and Children recommends universal newborn screening for SCD.
Most states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, and the Virgin Islands all provide universal screening for SCD.
USPSTF health screening recommendations and interventions are applicable to patients with SCD.
Secondary screening is recommended for strokes in children and for pulmonary hypertension, kidney function, retinopathy, liver assessment, and osteoporosis in adults.

Perform annual transcranial Doppler examinations for children with SCD, aged 2 to 16 years. Early transcranial Doppler screening and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) every 2 years after age 5 years with intensive therapy as needed (eg, transfusion for those with identified abnormalities, hydroxyurea) reduced the incidence of stroke by age 18 years from the previously reported 11% to 1.9% in a French study.

Doppler echocardiography can be used to screen for pulmonary hypertension (PH), however, the American Society of Hematology 2019 guidelines for SCD suggests against routine screening echocardiograms in asymptomatic children and adults with SCD. They suggest consideration of testing or consultation for patients in a steady state who have symptoms of resting dyspnea, hypoxemia or chest pain; dyspnea on exertion or exercise limitation out of proportion to their known condition; signs of heart failure, new heart murmur, or sleep-disordered breathing; or history of pulmonary embolism, presyncope or syncope or comorbid conditions associated with PH.
In one study, using a derived tricuspid regurgitant jet velocity cut-off of 2.88 m/sec (as opposed to 2.5 m/s) greatly increased specificity.

Refer to an ophthalmologist for a dilated eye examination to evaluate for retinopathy beginning at age 10 years. Based on a systematic review of 12 studies of patients with SCD, prevalence of sickle cell maculopathy was 45.6% and it increased with age.
Provide prenatal testing and family and genetic counseling.
Give pneumococcal vaccination to all patients as well as meningococcal, hepatitis B and influenza vaccination.

Authors of a meta-analysis of studies of invasive pneumococcal disease, however, found that most cases in children with SCD were due to serotypes that are not included in any of the licensed pneumococcal vaccines. In a recent phase 3 trial including 103 children with SCD, safety and immunogenicity were comparable for the 13-valent (Prevnar-13) and V114, a 15-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV).

Treat children prophylactically with twice daily penicillin (125 mg for those aged <3 years and 250 mg for those aged ≥3 years) until age 5 years, unless they have had a splenectomy or invasive pneumococcal infection. Prophylactic penicillin significantly reduces the risk of pneumococcal infection in children with SCD (low certainty). Adverse effects are rare and minor.

Based on a systematic review and meta-analysis of 41 studies, hemoglobin concentration was significantly lower in patients with SCD and cerebrovascular disease (0.4 g/dL), albuminuria (0.6 g/dL), elevated estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure (0.9 g/dL), and in patients who subsequently died (0.6 g/dL). Modeled increased hemoglobin concentrations of 1 g/dL or greater resulted in decreased risk of negative clinical outcomes of 41% to 64%.

Refer children with elevated transcranial Doppler velocity (≥200 cm/s) for long-term transfusion therapy to prevent stroke. Children with conditional Doppler velocity (170-199 cm/s) should be referred for evaluation by a specialist with expertise in long-term transfusion therapy. Authors of a Cochrane review of 5 RCTs (4 terminated early) concluded that long-term red blood cell transfusions may reduce the incidence of silent cerebral infarcts in children with abnormal transcranial Doppler velocities, but may have little or no effect on children with normal TCD velocities.

According to another Cochrane review, for children at higher risk of stroke who have not had previous long-term transfusions, long-term red cell transfusions reduce the risk of stroke (moderate-quality evidence) and may reduce the risk of other SCD-related complications (low-quality evidence).
Chronic transfusion may also reduce the risk of acute chest syndrome (ACS), but Cochrane authors found only a single RCT with 10 subjects.

The American Society of Hematology published SCD transfusion support guidelines in 2020. They suggest using automated red-cell exchange transfusion over simple transfusion or manual red-cell exchange in patients with SCD (all genotypes) receiving chronic transfusions (conditional very-low-quality evidence).
Hydroxyurea is the only approved drug for treatment of SCD. Hydroxyurea works by induction of fetal hemoglobin production by an unknown mechanism thereby diluting the concentration of HbS.

In adults with three or more severe vasoocclusive crises during a year, with pain or chronic anemia that interferes with usual activities, or with severe or recurrent ACS, hydroxyurea therapy is strongly recommended by US guidelines.

Consider hydroxyurea in patients who have had three or more hospitalizations in a year or episodes of ACS in the previous year. Studies show that hydroxyurea is underutilized. Although the usual starting dose is 15 to 20 mg/kg/day increased to 35 mg/kg/day, lower doses may be similarly effective.

A large multicenter study demonstrated that hydroxyurea therapy reduces the frequency of pain crisis, ACS, transfusions, and hospitalizations. The incidence of painful crisis decreased from 4.5 to 2.5 per year. Hydroxyurea appears to be safe and effective for patients with severe Hb-SS disease. Authors of a meta-analysis including 7 trials of hydroxyurea confirmed benefit of hydroxyurea at higher doses (30 mg/kg/day) or fixed doses (20 mg/kg/day) for preventing vaso-occlusive crisis, acute chest syndrome, and need for transfusion.

Authors of another meta-analysis of 10 observational studies and one small RCT found a low rate of stroke of 1% (95% CI 0-5%) for patients with SCD who received hydroxyurea; 18% (95% CI 3-40%) of patients on hydroxyurea had silent stroke and 24% (95% CIs 0.02-0.57) had adverse events attributed to hydroxyurea.

For high-risk children with abnormal Doppler velocities who have received at least 1 year of transfusions and have no MRA-defined severe vasculopathy, hydroxyurea treatment was noninferior to continued chronic transfusions for maintaining transcranial Doppler velocities and preventing primary stroke at 2 years. The most common serious adverse event was vaso-occlusive pain which occurred in five (8%) of patients randomized to hydroxyurea and three (2%) of patients randomized to transfusions.

In a trial in Africa, hydroxyurea with dose escalation (approximately 30 mg/kg/day) had superior clinical efficacy with respect to achieving a hemoglobin level of 9.0 g/dl or more and fewer clinical events compared to fixed-dose hydroxyurea (approximately 20 mg/kg/day), with equivalent safety. The trial was stopped early for demonstrated efficacy.

An RCT enrolled Nigerian children aged 5-12 years with SCD and abnormal transcranial Doppler velocities, comparing low-dose (10 mg/kg per day) or moderate-dose (20 mg/kg per day) oral hydroxyurea taken once daily. There were no differences in stroke incidence (3% vs. 5%, respectively), although all-cause hospitalization rates were higher in those on low-dose hydroxyurea (27.4 vs 16.1 per 100 person-years; incident rate ratio 1.71, 95% CI 1.15-2.57).
Early treatment of young children 9 to 18 months of age with hydroxyurea did not confer benefit on growth at 2 years in one RCT.
Monitor hydroxyurea use closely. It is teratogenic and therefore should not be used in women who may become pregnant or who are breast feeding.

Up-regulation of P-selectin in endothelial cells and platelets appears to contribute to the pathogenesis of vaso-occlusive and sickle cell-related pain crises. In a phase II RCT, crizanlizumab, an antibody against the adhesion molecule P-selectin, significantly lowered the rate of sickle cell-related pain crises compared to placebo (1.6 vs. 3.0 crises per year, respectively). The likelihood of uncomplicated crises was also lower (1.1 vs 2.9). Adverse drug effects include arthralgias, diarrhea, pruritus, vomiting, and chest pain.
Sildenafil failed to reduce priapism frequency by at least 50% in a small placebo-controlled RCT of men with recurrent priapism.
Prasugrel, an antiplatelet agent, was not helpful in reducing the frequency of of vaso-occlusive crises in children and adolescents.

In an RCT including 193 children with SCD comparing ticagrelor, a reversible P2Y12 inhibitor, to placebo for preventing vaso-occlusive crises, the trial was stopped at 4 months after failure to show benefit (yearly incidence of vaso-occlusive crises was 2.74 in the ticagrelor group and 2.60 in the placebo group).
A peripheral blood smear will demonstrate cells with the characteristic sickle shape. C
Diagnosis is made by hemoglobin electrophoresis demonstrating sickle hemoglobin of greater than 40%. C
The main symptom is pain. Patients often experience acute episodes of pain and daily chronic pain. A focused history to bring out the location, severity, and nature of the pain is essential.

The consensus-based AAPT Diagnostic Criteria for acute sickle cell disease (SCD) pain includes four core dimensions: SCD diagnosis; increased pain that lasts 2 or more hours and began in the past 10 days; one or more of tenderness to palpation, pain with movement, or decreased range of motion in the pain region; pain not entirely explained by specific physical exam findings (eg, leg ulcer). Other pain dimensions addressed by this group included common features/presentations, modulating factors, functional consequences and putative mechanisms.

Focus the history and physical on pain and pain relief, symptoms of anemia, and evidence of end-organ damage. Pay particular attention to joint pains, dyspnea, vision and hearing changes, and kidney disease, all of which may indicate chronic end-organ damage.
Chronic physical findings may include stunted growth and development, jaundice, hyposplenia or lack of a spleen.
Evaluate the following acute symptoms and findings further for their respective complications:

Chest pain, chest symptoms, and fever can be the first sign of acute chest syndrome (ACS, a vaso-occlusive crisis of the pulmonary vasculature identified by new onset of infiltrate in conjunction with one or more new respiratory symptoms to include fever, cough, excruciating chest pain, sputum production, dyspnea, or hypoxia).

A headache can be a sign of a stroke. However, in a cohort of 872 children with SCD, recurrent headaches and migraines were associated with low hemoglobin levels and high pain rates but not silent cerebral infarction. Headaches were a very common symptom in these children; over one third (36.4%) reported recurrent headaches and 15.1% reported migraines.
Priapism is a common complication in males and needs urgent treatment.
Right upper quadrant pain associated with jaundice is of concern for gallbladder disease.
Acute abdominal pain is of concern for splenic sequestration.
Vision changes may signify a retinal artery occlusion.
See .

Hyponatremia (plasma sodium concentration <135 mmol/L), in one study, was associated with increased risk of acute chest syndrome (ACS) (OR 1.95; 95% CI 1.20-3.17), red blood cell transfusion (OR 2.71; 95% CI 1.58-4.65), and increased hospital length of stay by 1.1. A decreasing sodium concentration was observed in patients with evolving ACS.

Several tests are used for screening purposes, including a complete blood count (CBC) that demonstrates anemia; a peripheral blood film that demonstrates sickled cells; and the "sickling screen" in which a hemolysate is exposed to a reducing agent; patients with sickle cell trait will also be positive for this last test.
Hemoglobin electrophoresis and cation exchange high-performance liquid chromatography are diagnostic for SCD.
A sickle solubility test is used as an adjunct to electrophoresis to help distinguish from other variant hemoglobins. DNA testing is used for prenatal diagnosis.

Sickle SCAN™, a point-of-care test, demonstrated 99% sensitivity and specificity using venous blood for the diagnosis of HbSS, HbAS, HbSC, HbAC, and HbAA in one study; similar results were achieved using capillary blood sampling.

Suspect ACS in children with SCD presenting with fever, shortness of breath, tachypnea, cough, or rales. In one retrospective emergency department chart review, use of these criteria identified 158 (85%) of ACS cases, while avoiding 825 CXRs. The addition of CXR for children with chest pain or who had a white blood cell count ≥18.75 × 109 /L or a history of ACS identified 181 (98%), while avoiding 430 CXRs. Prospective validation is needed
Order a chest X-ray if acute chest syndrome is suspected; patients typically have an infiltrate.
A systematic review of 6 studies with 625 patients found that point of care ultrasound was 92% sensitive and 89% specific (LR+ 8, LR- 0.09).
Pulse oximetry is unreliable for diagnosis of hypoxemia in children with SCD.
Order echocardiography if pulmonary hypertension is suspected.

A risk score using 4 variables - age, insurance status, triage pain score, and amount of opioids administered during the emergency department visit - was useful in identifying patients at high risk of 30-day revisit after discharge for vaso-occlusive crisis (areas under the curve 0.75).

Diagnosis is made by hemoglobin electrophoresis demonstrating sickle hemoglobin of greater than 40%. Electrophoresis will also determine the particular type of SCD and the percentage of fetal hemoglobin.
Be vigilant for symptoms of common complications: chest pain (acute chest syndrome), headache (stroke), iron overload, and leg ulcers.

For patients presenting with an acute pain episode, the National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) recommends monitoring for abnormal respiratory signs or symptoms, chest pain, fever, and hypoxia. Other complications that can be seen with patients in acute crisis include stroke, aplastic crisis, infection, osteomyelitis and splenic sequestration.
Patients presenting with a vaso-occlusive episode should be triaged at Emergency Severity Index (ESI) level 2 (i.e. high risk patient, needs medical attention as soon as possible)
Prompt and aggressive analgesic treatment is crucial. Early initiation of opioids has been shown to improve outcomes which may lead to earlier discharge from the ED and fewer hospitalizations.

NICE recommends that hospitalized patients with an acute painful sickle cell episode have a pain assessment, clinical assessment, and appropriate analgesia within 30 minutes of presentation. Once treatment is administered, pain relief should be assessed every 30 minutes until satisfactory relief has been achieved, and then at least every 4 hours.
Provide appropriate immunizations and screening.
For those with severe disease, including complications, discuss additional treatment options.
See for key elements in the management of acute sickle cell crisis.

Drug therapy for pain includes non-steroidal antinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), rapid initiation of opioids during a crisis, selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (sNRIs), tryciclic antidepressants (TCAs), gabapentinoids, ketamine, regional anesthesia and adjuvant treatments.B
Treating sickle cell pain with long-acting opioids decreases hospital admissions and emergency room use; oral opioids are preferred to IV opioids. B
Use psychological therapies routinely for patients with SCD. B

Hydroxyurea appears to be safe and effective for patients with severe Hb-SS disease and is indicated for patients who have 3 or more painful episodes per year and who have sickle cell complications (see Secondary Prevention). A
Consider HLA-matched related hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in patients with SCD who experienced a stroke, recurrent episodes of acute chest syndrome (ACS), frequent pain. B
Gene therapy is highly promising and is currently being studied in small uncontrolled trials. C

In patients with SCD, acute pain is likely multifactorial, including components such as hypoxia due to disease-induced vaso-occlusive crises, inflammation and neuropathic pain. Chronic pain affects 30-40% of people with SCD and probably has a complex biopsychosocial origin.

Treatments for SCD-related pain include non-steroidal antinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), opioids, selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (sNRIs), tryciclic antidepressants (TCAs), gabapentinoids, ketamine, regional anesthesia and adjuvant treatments.

For adults or chlidren presenting with acute pain, the American Society of Hematology (ASH) 2020 guidelines for sickle cell disease: management of acute and chronic pain evidence-based guideline recommends a tailored opioid therapy with or without a 5-7 days course of a NSAID, while it advices against corticosteroids (conditional recommendations). If pain remains uncontrolled and the patient is hospitalized, the expert panel suggest subanesthetic ketamine (0.1-0.3 mg/kg) or regional anesthesia in case of localized pain (conditional recommendations).Adjuvant treatments for acute pain include massage, yoga, trancutaneous nerve stimulation (TENS), virtual reality and guided relaxation (conditional recommendation, low certainty evidence).

For adults presenting with chronic pain, pharmacological treatment options include SNRIs (e.g. duloxetine), TCAs (e.g. amitriptyline) or gabapentinoids (conditional recommendations). These drugs are not recommended in children.

For adults or chlidren presenting with chronic pain the ASH guideline also suggests cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) in the context of a comprehensive disease management strategy. Guideline authors suggest not to initiate chronic opioids in patients with recently developed chronic pain (unless the pain is refractory to other treatments) or to stop chronic opioids if the patient is functioning poorly or is at high risk of developing an opioid use disorder. Finally, if the patient is already on chronic opioid therapy and the pain is well controlled, any decision to discontinue opioids should be made collaboratively between the physician and the patient (conditional recommendations).
A small trial including 111 adolescents (12-18 years of age), showed that CBT administered via a smartphone app may be effective in reducing chronic SCD-related pain.

NICE recommends a bolus dose of a strong opioid within 30 minutes of presentation for patients with a severe acute painful sickle cell episode or a moderately severe episode if pain medication has already been taken before presentation. If the patient is in moderate pain with no prior analgesia, use a weak opioid as an alternative or continue NSAIDs, if effective. If a patient continues to have severe pain at 30 minutes, offer a second bolus dose of a strong opioid. Consider patient-controlled analgesia if repeated doses of a strong opioid are needed over two hours. Laxatives, anti-emetics and antipruritics can be used as needed. The 2014 expert guidelines concur.

When opioids are used, oral opioids should be first-line treatment unless there is clinical evidence that the patient cannot take or absorb oral medications. Oral controlled-release morphine provides a safe and effective alternative to continuous IV morphine. For patients given strong opioids, NICE recommends monitoring for adverse events every hour for the first 6 hours after first administration or step up of pain relief and then at least every 4 hours. Authors of a Cochrane review were unable to find sufficient data to determine best pharmacological interventions for treat paining related to sickle cell vaso-occlusive crises in adults.

Use of an individualized pain protocol compared to standard weight-based dosing resulted in more rapid reduction in pain among adults with SCD in a RCT of 49 patients with 122 emergency department visits.

Based on a prospective cohort study, patients with SCD vaso-occlusive crisis treated in an infusion center vs. the emergency department had a shorter mean time to first dose of parenteral pain medication (62 minutes vs 132 minutes, respectively), were more likely to have their pain reassessed 30 minutes after their initial dose of pain medication, and were less likely to be admitted to the hospital (RR 0.25; 0.18 - 0.33). Of 444 enrolled patients in this study, 269 had 1441 acute care visits for an uncomplicated vaso-occlusive crisis during weekday daytime hours with a mean number of visits per patient of 5.4.

Single-dose ketamine infusion vs. morphine infusion over 30 minutes for adults with SDC presenting in vaso-occlusive crisis produced a similar reduction in numerical pain rating scale score over 2 hours and reduced the cumulative morphine dose. However, ketamine administration resulted in higher rates of drug-related side effects (6.3% vs. 2.2% in the morphine group), with similar rates of hospital admission.

Voxelotor, an HbS polymerization inhibitor, was evaluated in a phase 3 trial of patients with SCD, most also taking hydroxyurea. Voxelotor had disease-modifying effects with fewer intervention patients showing worsening anemia from baseline to 24 weeks and greater reductions from baseline in indirect bilirubin level and percentage of reticulocytes than the placebo group.

In a 72-week follow-up of the HOPE RCT, in which 274 patients with SCD were randomly assigned (1:1:1) to once-daily oral voxelotor 1500 mg, voxelotor 900 mg, or placebo, both doses of voxelotor significantly increased hemoglobin levels over placebo, with adjusted mean change in hemoglobin concentration from baseline of 1.0 g/dL (95% CI 0.7 to -1.3), 0.5 g/dL (0.3 to -0.8), and 0.0 g/dL (-0.3 to 0.3), respectively. Similar rates of serious adverse events unrelated to SCD were observed in each group (28%, 22% and 25%, respectively).
Inhaled nitric oxide, magnesium sulfate and IV acetaminophen were not effective in the management of SCS-related pain.

In a phase 2 trial, sevuparin, a novel non-anticoagulant low molecular weight heparinoid with anti-adhesive properties, did not reduce median time to vaso-occlusive crisis resolution compared to placebo (100.4 hours, 95% CI 85.5-116.8 vs. 86.4 hours, 95% CI 70.6-95.1). Serious adverse events occurred in 22% in each group (16 of 68 and 21 of 75, respectively).

Rivipansel, a predominantly E-selectin antagonist, was not effective for reducing time to readiness for discharge, time to discharge, time to discontinuation of IV opioids, or cumulative IV opioid use in a phase 3 trial. Authors note that reducing timing of initiation of treatment may make the drug more successful.

For children and adults with SCD and albuminuria the American Society of Hematology 2019 guidelines for SCD: cardiopulmonary and kidney disease suggest use of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin II receptor blockers (very-low-certainty evidence). For those with chronic kidney disease and worsening anemia, the guideline panel suggests combination therapy with hydroxyurea and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (very-low-certainty evidence).

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 3 RCTs and 3 retrospective cohort studies including 3,304 patients in vaso-occlusive crisis and 5,562 patients with ACS episodes found no difference between corticosteroids and standard treatment regarding overall transfusion requirement, the primary outcome of interest. Although corticosteroid use was associated with reduced length of hospital stay (mean difference -24 hours, 95% CI: -35 to -14), corticosteroids were associated with an increased risk of hospital readmission. There also appears to be a high rate of rebound pain upon discontinuation of steroids.

The American Society of Hematology 2020 guidelines for SCD transfusion recommend prophylactic red cell antigen matching for Rh (C, E or C/c, E/e) and K antigens over only ABO/RhD matching for patients with SCD (all genotypes) receiving transfusions. They suggest use of immuno-suppressive therapy (intravenous immunoglobulin [IVIg], steroids, and/or rituximab) in patients with SCD (all genotypes) with an acute need for transfusion and at high risk for acute hemolytic transfusion reaction or with a history of multiple or life-threatening delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions (very-low-certainty evidence).
Do not administer a blood transfusion unless there are other indications for transfusion in children and adults with a vaso-occlusive crisis.
Use simple transfusion to improve dyspnea, fatigue, and heart failure (see acute chest syndrome, acute stroke, and splenic sequestration above).

Use exchange transfusion to reduce the concentration of HB-S quickly in the case of acute complications. In one RCT, there was no significant benefit of automated red cell exchange over manual red cell exchange transfusion in reducing hemoglobin S percentage and attenuating serum ferritin level.
Conditions that can require surgical intervention include gallbladder disease, priapism, and splenic complications.
Recommendations for perioperative care of patients with SCD are available from a 2021 guideline prepared by a working group of the Association of Anaesthetists of Great Britain and Ireland.
Splenectomy may prevent further sequestration crisis, but there is currently a lack of evidence to show increased survival or decreased morbidity.

Avascular necrosis can be treated both surgically and nonsurgically. In one systematic review of 16 studies on total hip arthroplasty for hip osteonecrosis in patients with SCD, although there was reduced pain and functional improvement following surgery, patients with SCD compared to patients without SCD experienced higher readmission and revision rates, higher rates of surgical complications (e.g., wound complications and periprosthetic fracture) and medical complications (e.g., pain crises, ACS, cardiac complications, sepsis) and increased mortality.

The American Society of Hematology 2020 guidelines for SCD transfusion support suggest preoperative transfusion in patients with SCD undergoing surgeries requiring general anesthesia and lasting more than 1 hour (very-low-certainty evidence). Authors of a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to determine whether conservative preoperative blood transfusion is as effective as aggressive preoperative blood transfusion in preventing sickle-related or surgery-related complications in people with SCD. There is very low-quality evidence that preoperative blood transfusion may prevent development of ACS.

In patients with SCD and chronic pain, inhaled vaporized cannabis 3 times daily for 5 days was no better than placebo for reducing pain or associated symptoms with the exception of decreased interference with mood.
Two small RCTs found a benefit for Niprisan®, a phytochemical, in reducing the frequency of acute sickle cell crisis.

In a one-year RCT of 140 patients with SCD, omega-3 capsules containing 278 mg DHA and 39 mg EPA reduced the median rate of clinical vaso-occlusive events over placebo. In a 3-arm RCT including 165 children with SCD, 1000 mg omega-3 fish oil was more effective than placebo at reducing the number of pain crises over 10 months (one pain episode vs. 3 episodes, respectively) and pain levels (3 vs. 6 on a scale of 10, respectively). Although the vitamin D arm was also more effective than standard therapy, omega-3 was significantly more effective than vitamin D.

In a pilot study, high dose vitamin D at 4000 to 100,000 IU per week over 6 weeks vs. placebo decreased the number of pain days per week and improved physical activity quality-of-life scores. Authors of a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to evaluate potential benefit of vitamin D supplementation in patients for SCD based on the 3 available RCTs.
Physical therapy is a treatment option for chronic pain. In avascular necrosis, physical therapy is as effective in improving hip function as surgical procedures.

In an RCT of 58 adult patients with SCD hospitalized with pain, use of progressive muscle relaxation exercises for 30 minutes vs. rest improved mean pain scores at the third time point on days 1, 2, and 3, but had no effect on coping methods for pain, pain location, or complaints accompanying pain.
Authors of a Cochrane review were unable to determine potential benefit of transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation on SCD pain based on a single, very low-quality trial.
Use incentive spirometry during hospitalization for vaso-occlusive crisis to prevent ACS.

Psychological therapies, especially relaxation and cognitive behavioral therapy, are effective in reducing the severity and frequency of headaches in children and adolescents and pain and disability from non-headache pain, including pain associated with SCD.
Psychological treatment can help improve patient understanding of the disease and may be helpful for chronic pain syndromes, anxiety, and depression.

In an RCT of 47 children with SCD and short-term memory or working memory difficulties, those randomized to Cogmed Working Memory Training at home on a tablet device vs. wait-listing had greater improvement in visual working memory. Children who completed 10 or more training sessions (N=19) also demonstrated improvements in verbal short-term memory and math fluency.
Educate patients on maintaining an ideal body weight to avoid stress associated with obesity, which may adversely affect their disease.
The addition of a community health worker for patients with SCD taking hydroxyurea did not result in hematological improvements at 12 months despite behavioral improvements in medication adherence.

In a before and after study, use of a multimodal intervention including standardized admission orders, monthly house staff education, and patient and caregiver education increased use of patient-controlled analgesia (73% vs. 52%) and decreased the occurrence of ACS (12% vs. 25%) among children with SCD admitted for pain.
Instruct patients to avoid extremes of temperature, which can initiate a crisis, to dress appropriately when outside, and to avoid swimming in cold water.
Encourage exercise, but instruct patients to avoid dehydration and excessive stress.
Extra oral or intravenous fluids are routinely administered to patients during acute painful vaso-occlusive crises, but there are no RCTs supporting this practice.

HSCT as a treatment for SCD has not been studied in RCTs. The American Society of Hematology released guidelines in 2021 on use of HSCT. The panel, which included 2 patient partners, provided conditional recommendations, based on low to very low-certainty evidence, to help patients and providers consider the timing and type of HSCT for individuals with SCD. The panel suggests that HLA-matched related HSCT be used rather than standard of care (hydroxyurea (HU)/transfusion) in patients with SCD who have experienced an overt stroke or have an abnormal transcranial Doppler ultrasound. In patients with frequent pain or recurrent ACS, the panel suggests using related matched allogeneic transplantation rather than standard of care (and at an earlier age, if possible; in these cases, the panel suggests using either total-body irradiation ≤400 cGy or chemotherapy-based conditioning regimens. For patients with SCD and an indication for HSCT, but who lack a matched sibling donor, the ASH guideline panel suggests using transplants from alternative donors in the context of a clinical trial. Additional recommendations can be found in the cited guideline.

Survival after HLA-identical sibling donor HSCT varies by age. In a large retrospective analysis of HSCT in patients with SCD, mortality ranged from 5%-20%. Other adverse effects include acute graft-versus-host disease (GVHD, 16%) and chronic GVHD (23%), infection, infertility, and a low risk of therapy-related malignancy.

Among 1425 patients with SCD undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation, two factors were predictive for event-free survival (EFS): age at transplantation and donor type. Those aged 12 years or younger with an HLA-matched sibling donor had the best outcomes (3-year EFS of 92%).

In a cohort study of 28 children with SCD who had a matched sibling donor and underwent HSCT and 32 children with SCD without a matched donor maintained on standard care, no children developed cerebral artery stenosis following HSCT vs. 2 on standard care at 3-year follow-up. Of the 14 patients with stenosis on study entry, only five in the HSCT arm still had stenosis at 3 years vs. 10 patients on standard care.

For those without a matched sibling donor, haploidentical related donors can be considered for transplantation. Authors of a meta-analysis of 3 studies that included both haploidentical and matched sibling donor transplantation, found graft failure to be significantly higher in the haploidentical group (OR 5.3, 95% CI 1.0 to 27.6). However, overall survival was high (91%) and not significantly different between type of transplantation. Further, patients undergoing haploidentical SCT had relatively low overall pooled proportions of graft failure (7%; 95% CI, 2% to 20%), acute GVHD (4%; 95% CI, 2% to 12%), and chronic GVHD (11%; 95% CI, 7% to 16%).

Lovotibeglogene autotemcel (LentiGlobin) is an autologous transplant of hematopoietic stem cells encoded with the BB305 lentiviral vector that modifies the β-globin gene and results in production of an antisickling hemoglobin. In a Phase 1/2 trial with 35 patients, patients given the intervention had a significant increase in hemoglobin (from 8.5 to 11 gm/dl) with resolution of vaso-occlusive events that had been occurring a median of 3.5 times in the 2 years before treatment.

Gene editing is also under investigation. In two patients, one with SCD, myeloablation followed by administration of autologous CD34+ cells edited with CRISPR-Cas9 targeting the BCL11A enhancer resulted in high levels of allelic editing in bone marrow and blood, pancellular increases in fetal hemoglobin, transfusion independence, and (in the patient with SCD) elimination of vaso-occlusive episodes over 1 year. Similar gene therapy using BCL11A inhibition as an effective target was effective in 6 patients in increasing percentage of fetal hemoglobin which was broadly distributed in red blood cells at 18 months.

Authors of the largest case series of 44 patients with severe SCD treated these patients using exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel), an autologous cell therapy that reactivates fetal hemoglobin production using gene editing with clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)–Cas9 technology in red blood cells. Prior to therapy, the average number of vaso-occlusive crises per year in the previous 2 years was 4.1 and at 16 or more months follow up for 30 patients, 29 (97%) had no severe vaso-occlusive crises for at least 12 months and none were hospitalized.
Comprehensive care is a lifelong process.
Hospitalize patients for vaso-occlusive pain that is uncontrolled with oral medications, as well as for chest pain, shortness of breath, or hypoxia to exclude the possibility of acute chest syndrome.
Hospitalize for an acute drop in hemoglobin.
Evaluate acute abdominal pain urgently.
Treat prolonged priapism urgently.

Prevalence of central nervous system complications in children with SCD include silent cerebral infarcts (39% by 18 years), headache (36%), ischemic stroke (as low as 1% in children undergoing effective screening and prophylaxis and ∼11% in children without screening), and hemorrhagic stroke (3%). Authors of a meta-analysis of 69 studies found a prevalence of silent cerebral infarcts ranging between 20% and 50% in most studies.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 16 studies of patients with SCD in which cognitive function was measured using Wechsler Intelligence Scales found significantly lower full-scale intelligence quotients for those with overt stroke vs. controls of -12.6 (p < .001) and silent cerebral infarct vs. controls of -5.7 (p < .001).

In a systematic review of neurologic complications from 31 studies of patients from Africa with SCD, prevalence rates were 18.9% for headache, 4.4% for seizures and 4.2% for stroke. Data quality, however, was poor.
Use blood transfusions or HSCT for patients who have had ischemic strokes, recurrent pain episodes, and acute complications.
Acute stroke: Consult a sickle cell disease expert and perform exchange transfusion.
Venous thromboembolism (VTE): VTE is frequent in patients with SCD; in a cross-sectional study of 404 patients with SCD, one quarter had a history of VTE with a median age at diagnosis of 30 years.

For adults with SCD and first unprovoked VTE, the American Society of Hematology 2019 guidelines suggest indefinite anticoagulation (low-certainty evidence). For adults with SCD and first provoked VTE, the guidelines suggest 3-6 months of anticoagulation.

Recurrence rates of VTE are also high. In a study of 877 SCD patients with an incident VTE, the cumulative incidence of recurrent VTE at 1 and 5 years was 13.2% (95% CI 11.0%-15.5%) and 24.1% (95% CI 21.2%-27.1%). Risk factors for recurrence were more severe SCD (HR 2.41, CI 1.67-3.47), incident lower extremity DVT (HR 1.64, CI 1.17-2.30), and pneumonia/ACS (HR 1.68, CI 1.15-2.45).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 studies found an overall recurrence of VTE of 27.6% (95%CI 23.5-31.9) among patients who were anticoagulated following a VTE. The overall rate of pulmonary embolism was 11.7% (95%CI 4.3-22.1), overall bleeding rate was 14.1% (95%CI 7.8-21.9) and overall mortality rate was 3.7% (95%CI 0.8-8.5).
SCD is associated with both acute and recurrent ischemic priapism.

Hydration and oral or IV analgesia is recommended based on consensus and consultation with a urologist (and hematologist, if surgery is planned for preoperative transfusion). Several therapies are available for priapism, but evidence is limited regarding risks and benefits of any of them.

The American Urologic Association/ Sexual Medicine Society of North America 2021 guideline on priapism recommends relieving an episode of ischemic priapism in patients with SCD with prompt intracavernosal phenylephrine and corporal aspiration, with or without irrigation, before proceeding to systemic therapies (expert opinion). They recommend against use of exchange transfusion as the primary treatment (expert opinion). Patients with SCD should be advised to present for urologic evaluation for priapism episodes of >4 hours, so that detumescence can be induced before permanent corporal damage occurs.
Among children with SCD, those with ACS have lower total lung capacity at baseline and at 2 years and poorer lung function than children without ACS.

Treat ACS, one of the most feared complications, with intravenous cephalosporin; an oral macrolide antibiotic; rapid initiation of opioids for severe pain; supplemental oxygen to maintain oxygen saturation of >95%; and close monitoring for bronchospasm, acute anemia, and hypoxemia. Other treatments are respiratory therapy including incentive spirometry, pain management, and bronchodilators. However, no trials have addressed the use of bronchodilators for ACS. Similarly, while inhaled nitric oxide has been recommended for ACS, clinical trials are lacking.

Based on weak evidence, give simple blood transfusion (10 mL/kg of red blood cells) to improve oxygen carrying capacity to persons who are symptomatic and have a hemoglobin concentration >1.0 g/dL below baseline; if baseline hemoglobin is ≥9 g/dL, however, simple blood transfusion may not be required.

Pulmonary hypertension (PH): Treat PH with hydroxyurea as primary therapy and transfusions as an alternate. There are limited data supporting sildenafil. No PH-specific treatment is suggested unless the patient has confirmed PH by right heart catheterization and elevated pulmonary vascular resistance and normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure; in these cases, there is a weak recommendation for either a prostacyclin agonist or endothelin receptor antagonist therapy. Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor therapy should not be used.

Transfusion reaction: The American Society of Hematology 2020 guidelines for SCD transfusion suggests immunosuppressive therapy (IVIg, steroids, rituximab, and/or eculizumab) over no immunosuppressive therapy in patients with SCD (all genotypes) with a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction and ongoing hyperhemolysis (very-low-certainty evidence about effects).

Iron overload: Treat iron overload secondary to chronic transfusions with iron chelation. The oral chelator deferasirox appears to have good efficacy, and appears to be as effective as deferoxamine. Efficacy regarding patient-important outcomes, however, is limited.

In a phase 3 study of 435 children with transfusion-dependent hemoglobinopathies, 7% with SCD, deferiprone was non-inferior to deferasirox. Treatment success as measured by change in serum ferritin and T2-weighted cardiac MRI was 69/125 (55.2%) in patients assigned to deferiprone vs 80/146 (54.8%) for those assigned to deferasirox at 1 year.

In a 2-year extension of the Ferriprox in Patients With Iron Overload in Sickle Cell Disease Trial (FIRST), a one-year, randomized noninferiority study of deferiprone vs deferoxamine, the most common side effects among the 134 patients who continued deferiprone at a mean of 2.1 (0.8) years were neutropenia (9.0%) and abdominal pain (7.5%). Mean serum ferritin levels decreased significantly after year 2 (-771, P = .0008) and year 3 (-1016, P = .0420) with responder rates, defined as ≥20% improvement in efficacy measure, increasing each year from 35.2% in year 1 to 70.9% in year 3.

Leg ulcer: Treat leg ulcers with avoidance of trauma, supportive dressings, elevation, and physiotherapy. The topical preparation RGD peptide matrix reduced ulcer size in patients with SCD but not the incidence of complete closure over the control group. Antibiotics should be added if infection is suspected and wound culture is positive and the organisms are susceptible. Evaluate patients with chronic recalcitrant deep ulcers for osteomyelitis.
Splenic sequestration: Immediate IV fluid resuscitation and consultation with clinical expert about avoiding overtransfusion and need for splenectomy.

Invasive pneumococcal disease: prevalence is 1.9% (95% CI 1.7-2.2%) based on a meta-analysis of 16 studies with 9438 children up to age 22 years with SCD. The most common presentation in this study was septicemia (84/137; 61%) followed by lower respiratory tract infection (29%) and meningitis (9%). The crude case fatality rate was 21/182 (11.5%, 95% CI, 7.3-17.1%). Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 studies of febrile patients with SCD found a weighted prevalence of bacteremia across all studies was 1.9% (95% CI 1.22%-2.73%), and for Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteremia of 0.31% (95% CI 0.16%-0.50%).
Microalbuminuria: For adults with microalbuminiuria, use an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor.
Acute renal failure: Use renal replacement therapy when needed, monitor daily, avoid nephrotoxic agents, and seek potential etiologies.

Avascular necrosis: Evaluate patients with intermittent or chronic hip pain by history, physical examination, radiography, and magnetic resonance as needed, and treat with analgesics and physical therapy. Cochrane authors found no evidence that adding hip core decompression to physical therapy achieved clinical improvement in people with SCD and avascular necrosis compared to physical therapy alone based on a single trial.
Ophthalmologic: Refer patients with vitreoretinal complications of proliferative sickle retinopathy for possible vitrectomy or laser treatment.

The standard of care for treating acute vaso-occlusive pain episodes includes frequent pain intensity assessments and rapid availability of rescue analgesia. The American Pain Society has published clinical practice guidelines for the management of sickle cell pain.
Use of a hospital-developed evidence-based ACS/SCD guideline for children admitted for SCD reduced hospital length of stay and costs.
Routine lab work and studies include a CBC, reticulocyte count, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), comprehensive metabolic panel, and CXR.

Use IV hydration and opioids in the initial management of an acute painful crisis in the hospital. Patient-controlled analgesia has been shown to be just as good for pain relief as continuous infusion, with lower overall use of opioids and a decrease in overall length of hospital stay.
Incentive spirometry has been shown to decrease pulmonary complications.
Monitor oxygen saturation closely. Supplemental oxygen is not indicated unless there is documented hypoxemia.

In general, transfuse patients to achieve hemoglobin greater than 10 g/L for operative procedures. Data are limited on the benefits of aggressive transfusions preoperatively. (see Surgery section above)
Provide appropriate DVT prophylaxis.
The median age of survival is 42 years for males with HB-SS, 48 years for females with HB-SS, 60 years for males with HB-SC, and 68 years for females with HB-SC. B
Patients who have more episodes of pain have a lower life expectancy. B
The average patient experiences approximately 1 vaso-occlusive episode per year; a few have 6 or more episodes per year. B

SCD used to be primarily a pediatric disease, and in the 1970s the life expectancy was approximately 20 years. When untreated, most children will not survive into adulthood; 90% of children in sub-Saharan Africa do not survive past the age of 3 years.
Most patients will experience episodes of acute pain. The typical sickle cell crisis lasts for 10 days.
The average patient experiences approximately 1 vaso-occlusive episode per year. A small percentage of patients have more than 6 episodes per year.
As patients age, they will progressively develop end-organ damage. The main organs affected are the kidneys, bones and joints, heart, lungs, eyes, and brain.

In the United States, the most recently available data for median age of survival show 42 years for males with HB-SS, 48 years for females with HB-SS, 60 years for males with HB-SC, and 68 years for females with HB-SC.
Patients who have higher numbers of painful episodes have a lower life expectancy.

Risk of early death is associated with multiple pain episodes, anemic events, ACS, and pulmonary hypertension. In addition, those with significant tricuspid regurgitant velocity (>2.5 m/sec on echocardiography) and elevated serum N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide level (>160 pg/ml) are also at higher risk or mortality.
Upon hospital discharge for an acute painful sickle cell episode, patients should be given information on how to continue to manage their current episode.
Every 3 months, assess steady-state lab values and give appropriate preventive treatment.
Routinely asses the CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, LDH, reticulocyte count, and urine microalbumin.

For patients receiving chronic transfusion therapy, the American Society of Hematology 2020 guidelines for SCD transfusion suggest iron overload screening by magnetic resonance imaging for liver iron content every 1 to 2 years vs. serial monitoring of ferritin levels alone (very-low-certainty evidence). This is also endorsed by NHLBI guidelines.
Follow patients treated chronically with opioids more closely.

Patients are best served in a comprehensive sickle cell center. A multidisciplinary team should be involved, including a primary care physician, a hematologist, a psychologist or psychiatrist, a nurse, and a social worker.

A useful resource for patients and providers is the Sickle Cell Disease Educational Repository, a product of the HRSA-funded Sickle Cell Disease Newborn Screening Follow-up Program which is comprised of seventeen community-based organization partnerships.
Patients should be encouraged to take an active role in their care.
Sickle cell anemia in the elderly has not been well studied.

Pregnant women are considered to be at high risk of maternal death (72.4/100,000 deliveries), maternal morbidity (e.g., higher rates of cerebral vein thrombosis, pneumonia, pyelonephritis, deep venous thrombosis, transfusion, postpartum infection, and sepsis), preterm birth (OR 1.5; 95% CI = 1.2, 1.8), fetal death (OR 2.2; 95% CI = 1.2, 4.2) and severe fetal anemia and need to be closely followed by both an obstetrician and a hematologist.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis that included 3964 pregnancies in women with SCD found a prevalence of ACS and pneumonia of 6.46% (95% CI 4.66% -8.25%). The risk of pulmonary thromboembolism was also increased compared to control women (RR 7.74; 95% CI 4.65-12.89).

The usefulness of prophylactic blood transfusion to improve obstetric or perinatal outcomes is unclear. Authors of a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to support prophylactic blood transfusion. Authors of another meta-analysis of 12 trials found prophylactic transfusions positively associated with a reduction in maternal mortality, vaso-occlusive pain episodes, pulmonary complications, perinatal mortality, and neonatal prematurity and death, although the studies were small, with methodologic limitations.
Transcranial Doppler ultrasound is recommended to screen all children, aged 2 to 16 years, with SCD for cerebrovascular disease.

Evaluate children with fever and other signs of infection promptly. In one retrospective study of 1118 febrile episodes among children with SCD, however, bacteremia was infrequent (0.8%; 95% CI = 0.3%-1.3%).
Evaluate pain urgently.
Treat children prophylactically with penicillin.

Data on corticosteroid use for chest pain or ACS in children are limited to two studies from the same institution that found shorter duration of analgesic use (41.3 vs. 71.3 and 19 vs. 76 hours), but more patients readmitted for rebound pain (4 vs. 0-1).

list.listitem: Check vital signs, CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, reticulocyte count, and oxygenation saturation (in adults). If chronic pain exists, refer for outpatient management of chronic pain. If severe anemia is present, admit and evaluate for aplastic crisis.
If patient has chest pain, shortness of breath, or hypoxemia: urgent evaluation for acute chest syndrome.
If abdominal pain is present: evaluate for splenic or liver sequestration or gallbladder disease.
Treat pain with oral medications: NSAIDS and or opioids and adjuvant pain medications. Reassess hourly.

If pain remains uncontrolled after several treatments; admit and treat with IV medications. Consult hematology if suspicion exists for a sickle cell complication. Treat with IV fluids and incentive spirometer. Evaluate pain regularly. Check CXR and daily CBC.
If pain is controlled and vital signs are stable: discharge to home and continue treatment as an outpatient with close follow-up.

Once admitted, treat with IV opioids using patient-controlled anesthesia when possible. Begin to convert to oral opioids within 24 to 48 hours unless there is clinical evidence of failure to tolerate oral medications. Convert to oral opioids using equianalgesic dosing principles. Observe for additional 24 hours once on oral medication before discharge. Taper opioid medications as outpatient. Follow closely after discharge.
